summary:
Putumayo department stands under Colombia's national framework, which is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement. Marriage equality has been available since 2016, adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, and national identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025. A comprehensive trans law was still under legislative consideration in 2025.

Enforcement lags far behind that framework. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders in Colombia between January and May 2025 alone. The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025, praising the government's legal reforms and commitment to equality while warning that institutional progress and daily lived experience are disconnected, and that widespread discrimination and violence against LGBT people must be addressed urgently as killings rise.

The pattern most relevant to a trans visitor in Putumayo is armed-group social control in territories where the state's presence is thin. In Caquetá department, armed groups circulated "social cleansing" flyers on the streets and through WhatsApp naming "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets, a campaign run by groups still operating despite the 2016 peace agreement. Three armed men told trans woman Tatiana Cespedes, 51, she had one week to leave town or be killed; she hid for a week and then fled at night. In Guajira department, armed groups posted flyers from March 2024 carrying a kill list of named individuals under the wording "All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans".

The national tolls give the scale of the risk. At least 41 trans women were killed in Colombia in 2023, eight between February and April 2024, and 13 trans people in the first quarter of 2025. Targeted killings also continue in ordinary urban settings: Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was attacked in Bello, Antioquia in April 2025, and a video of the assault went viral from 5 April, showing her with fractured legs, arms and hands flailing in a creek unable to swim before she drowned. No one was arrested although police interrogated local residents. President Gustavo Petro ordered an urgent investigation, and solidarity events were held in several cities to denounce transphobia.

Some of this violence has been prosecuted as an international crime rather than ordinary homicide. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging that conflict-driven violence against these individuals constitutes gender persecution, a crime against humanity. The UN Human Rights Committee has registered concern over the same pattern. A Colombian court has separately ruled on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty, protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system.

Conviction rates in anti-LGBTQ killings run near 2% against 9% for homicides overall. A trans visitor to Putumayo should therefore expect the country-wide combination of armed-group social control in parts of the periphery, near-total impunity and episodic central-government response, rather than any documented department-level protection mechanism.
tangentialFactors:
Economic marginalisation shapes the exposure. Discrimination limits trans women in the departments where armed groups are active mainly to hairdressing or sex work, and the same reporting notes few options beyond sex work for trans women in Caquetá. A visitor who is read as trans may be assumed to fall into the same narrow economic category.

Threats produce displacement directly. Tatiana Cespedes, a trans salon owner, was forced to relocate twice after receiving death threats from armed men, and a friend of the trans woman Yesenia Rodríguez was killed.

The pattern of fatal attacks is not confined to armed-group zones or to trans victims. Reported cases include gay men lured through an app and killed, a trans rough-sleeper stabbed while sleeping, and people killed in their homes or in a hairdresser.

The gap between statute and practice is the comparison that matters: Colombia's notary-based marker change, court-recognised self-identification and hate-crime framework sit alongside a national homicide-resolution deficit and rising killings, a divergence the UN Independent Expert flagged explicitly in May 2025.

outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory reports a Putumayo-specific finding. The department-level evidence available concerns Caquetá, Guajira and Antioquia, so the assessment rests on the national pattern and on the armed-group threat model that applies across territories where such groups operate.

The conviction-rate comparison, near 2% for anti-LGBTQ killings against 9% for homicides overall, is not attributed to a source in this inventory and should be treated as unresolved.

Whether the comprehensive trans law put before the legislature in 2025 has since been enacted is unresolved in the sources.

Whether any department-level police protocol, protection programme or local oversight body operates in Putumayo is not sourced here.

The inventory does not establish the current strength or territorial control of armed groups within Putumayo itself; the documented flyer and ultimatum campaigns come from other departments.
